questions.prompt: Step size of a 10-bit ADC with a 3.3 V reference, in millivolts. Precision 0.005.
A 12-bit ADC with a 3.3 V reference returns 1000. Voltage at the pin in volts. Precision 0.002.
10-byte frames at 500 Hz on a 115200 baud 8N1 UART. Load as a fraction. Precision 0.002.
A 6-byte I2C register read on a 400 kHz bus (9 x (6 + 3) clocks). Time in microseconds. Precision 0.5.
The 6-byte read is repeated at 200 Hz on a 100 kHz bus. Bus load as a fraction. Precision 0.002.
Length in bits of a classic CAN data frame with 4 data bytes, no stuffing, including intermission.
Standard-mode I2C: rise time 1000 ns, bus capacitance 300 pF. Maximum pull-up in ohms (0.8473 formula). Precision 20.
A 5 V I2C bus with VOL 0.4 V at 3 mA. Minimum pull-up in ohms. Precision 5.
Which bus needs one extra select wire for every additional device?
options: I2C, since each device needs its own clock.
SPI, since the host picks a device with its chip-select line.
UART, since each device needs its own baud rate.
CAN, since each node needs its own terminator.
questions.explanation: SPI shares SCLK, MOSI and MISO and uses one chip-select line per device.

questions.prompt: Two UART devices exchange only garbage characters. Which cause is most likely?
options: The pull-ups are too weak for the bus capacitance.
The chip-select line is held high by the other device.
Both devices share the same bus address.
The ends use different baud rates.
questions.explanation: UART has no clock or address, so both ends must be set to the same baud rate; also check TX to RX and common ground.

questions.prompt: An I2C sensor works at 100 kHz on the desk but fails at 400 kHz on the robot's long cable. What is the likely cause?
options: Extra cable capacitance slows the rise time.
The sensor's address changes when a longer cable is fitted.
The ADC reference voltage is too low for the sensor.
The CAN bus terminator is missing from the cable.
questions.explanation: Rise time is about 0.8473 x Rp x Cb. More capacitance slows the edge; use stronger pull-ups, a lower speed or shorter wires.

questions.prompt: A robot must run a neural-network detector on a 30 fps camera and also close fast motor loops. Which split fits best?
options: An 8-bit MCU on its own, with no Linux.
An ESP32 on its own, using Wi-Fi to talk.
A GPU module for vision plus an MCU for motors.
One Raspberry Pi doing both jobs in Python.
questions.explanation: Neural-network inference wants a GPU class module; the deadline-bound motor loops belong on an MCU.

questions.prompt: Which statement about ESP32 and Arduino Uno pins is right?
options: Both are 5 V tolerant, so level shifting is never needed.
Uno logic is 5 V; ESP32 logic is 3.3 V, not 5 V tolerant.
The ESP32 reads 5 V inputs safely through its own ADC.
Both use 3.3 V logic and 10-bit ADCs on every pin.
questions.explanation: Uno: 5 V logic and a 10-bit ADC. ESP32: 3.3 V logic, 12-bit ADC, inputs not 5 V tolerant.

questions.prompt: In a control loop, what does jitter mean?
options: The average speed of the CPU clock in MHz.
The size of the program stored in flash memory.
The number of wires that the bus needs.
Timing variation between iterations.
questions.explanation: Jitter is timing variation. A hard real-time loop keeps it small compared with its period.

questions.prompt: A bus plan loads a link to 90 %. What is the best judgement?
options: Too tight: aim for 50 % to 70 % or less.
Fine: only loads above 100 % can cause any problem.
Fine: a busier link is always a faster link.
Too loose: raise the rate until the link reaches 100 %.
questions.explanation: Real links need headroom for retries, arbitration and jitter.
